qs.q: A 52-year-old chronic smoker presents with progressive dyspnea and emphysema. Serum protein electrophoresis reveals a marked absence of the alpha-1 band. Which specific biochemical property of the deficient protein normally protects lung parenchyma?
o: Neutralizing bacterial endotoxins entering the respiratory tract
Scavenging of reactive oxygen species generated by macrophages
Chelating extracellular copper ions to prevent tissue damage
Inhibition of neutrophil elastase activity via active binding
Regulating surfactant phospholipid turnover within the alveoli
qs.e: Alpha-1-antitrypsin is a serine protease inhibitor that protects lung elastic tissue by neutralizing neutrophil elastase.

qs.q: A 70-year-old male presents with bone pain and skull lesions. Serum protein electrophoresis reveals an M-protein spike, and a bone marrow biopsy shows sheets of atypical plasma cells with eccentric nuclei and clock-face chromatin. Which additional finding is typical of this condition?
o: Presence of ringed sideroblasts within developing erythroid precursors
Marked elevation of serum polyclonal immunoglobulins across classes
Excretion of Bence Jones proteins composed of free light chains
Decreased serum calcium levels due to enhanced bone formation
Marked peripheral blood thrombocytosis driven by elevated interleukins
qs.e: Multiple myeloma features clonal plasma cells producing monoclonal immunoglobulins and free light chains (Bence Jones proteins).

qs.q: A patient with suspected osteoporosis undergoes baseline laboratory studies to rule out secondary causes. Which condition should be evaluated using serum protein electrophoresis?
qs.e: Serum protein electrophoresis is used to check for multiple myeloma, which may be associated with osteoporosis. Thyroid dysfunction, vitamin D levels, and male hypogonadism are assessed using TSH, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and testosterone/gonadotropins respectively.

qs.q: A 55-year-old man presents with visual disturbances, fatigue and epistaxis. Serum protein electrophoresis shows a monoclonal IgM spike. Bone marrow biopsy reveals lymphoplasmacytoid infiltration. What gene mutation is present in >90% of cases?
qs.e: This is Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia (LPL). MYD88 mutation is present in >90% and is near-diagnostic.

exam: A 58‑year‑old man with back pain and weight loss has a 4‑cm M‑spike on SPEP. What is the next step? — Perform serum free light chain assay and bone marrow biopsy to confirm multiple myeloma.
A patient with HIV presents with a broad gamma band on SPEP. What does this suggest? — Poly‑clonal hypergammaglobulinaemia due to chronic immune activation.
A 45‑year‑old woman has a 1‑cm IgA M‑spike and normal calcium. What is the likely diagnosis? — IgA myeloma; monitor for progression with repeat SPEP and free light chains.
A child with sickle cell disease shows hypo‑albuminaemia on SPEP. What is the most probable cause? — Protein‑losing nephropathy secondary to sickle cell nephropathy.
A patient with hepatitis B has an elevated alpha‑2‑macroglobulin band. What does this indicate? — Chronic liver inflammation; monitor liver function and viral load.
A 70‑year‑old man with a 2‑cm M‑spike and creatinine 2.5 mg/dL has a high beta‑2‑microglobulin. What stage of myeloma is he in? — Stage III (high tumour burden).
ai.title: Serum Protein Electrophoresis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) separates serum proteins by charge and size, revealing abnormal monoclonal spikes that indicate plasma cell dyscrasias, liver disease, or protein loss. It guides diagnosis, staging and monitoring.

b: Used to screen for multiple myeloma, Waldenström macroglobulinemia, and other plasma cell disorders.
Also detects hypo‑albuminaemia, protein‑losing nephropathies and liver dysfunction.
sections.p: SPEP is a bedside‑friendly test that separates serum proteins into albumin, alpha‑1, alpha‑2, beta, and gamma fractions. A sharp monoclonal peak (M‑spike) in the gamma region is the hallmark of a monoclonal gammopathy.

t.b: A sharp, narrow peak in the gamma region (M‑spike).
In light‑chain myeloma or when SPEP is negative but suspicion remains high.

b: Monoclonal spike = one clone of plasma cells producing identical immunoglobulin.
Poly‑clonal increase = chronic inflammation or infection.
sections.p: The electrophoretic pattern reflects protein charge and size. Albumin migrates fastest; gamma proteins are the slowest. Monoclonal proteins appear as a single, intense band.

t.b: Possible IgA myeloma or chronic infection.
It correlates with tumour burden and renal function.

b: TB and schistosomiasis may raise alpha‑2‑macroglobulin.
sections.p: In East Africa, SPEP is often limited to tertiary centres. Clinicians must interpret results with local disease prevalence: HIV, TB, malaria, hepatitis B, schistosomiasis, and sickle cell can alter protein patterns.

t.b: Serum protein immunofixation or a urine Bence‑Jones protein test.

b: A narrow M‑spike in a patient with back pain and anemia should prompt a full myeloma work‑up.
sections.p: Examiners often ask how SPEP fits into the diagnostic work‑up and how to interpret atypical patterns. Focus on the clinical context and the need for confirmatory tests.

t.b: Significant monoclonal protein load, likely symptomatic myeloma.

b: Assuming any gamma rise is monoclonal.
sections.p: Clinicians often misinterpret a poly‑clonal rise as a monoclonal spike or ignore the need for immunofixation when SPEP is abnormal.
